newsitem.title: CHINA: China blasts U.S. for fighter sales to Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China blasts U.S. for fighter sales to Taiwan.

text.p: China blasted the United States on Wednesday for sales of F-16 fighters to Taiwan, saying the move had seriously harmed relations.
"The Chinese government has already voiced its strong opposition to the U.S. side," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said in a statement.

Speaking a day after Taiwan took delivery of two F-16s, Shen urged Washington to abide by a 1982 Sino-U.S. communique calling for the reduction in quality and quantity of arms sold by the United States to Taiwan.

"Now the U.S. side, in spite of the opposition and representations from the Chinese side, has persisted with conducting its erroneous decision and the Chinese side voices its strong dissatisfaction and resolute opposition," he said.
"(The Chinese side) has made solemn representations to the U.S. side," Shen said.
"(This) has seriously harmed the great task of the Chinese people to reunify the motherland and also seriously damaged Sino-U.S. relations," he said.
Taiwan took delivery on Tuesday of the first two of 150 F-16s that the island has bought to upgrade its defences.
China, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since the two split after a civil war in 1949, vows to retake the island eventually -- by force if necessary.

The United States defended its sale of the advanced fighters to Taiwan, saying the sale was fully consistent with communiques governing Sino-U.S. ties because the sale was for defensive purposes only.
Taiwan ordered the 150 jets from the United States in a deal approved in 1992 by former U.S. President George Bush.
The United States severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan and established ties with China in 1979, but it maintains close unofficial links with the island.
In Taipei, Taiwan's National Security Bureau chief said on Wednesday Taiwan and China were not likely to have a military confrontation in the next five years.

State radio quoted bureau director-general Yin Chung-wen as telling parliament that China's communist rulers were unlikely to launch military adventures in the Taiwan Strait that divides them in the coming five years.
However, Yin cautioned that with continued military buildups in China and Nationalist-ruled Taiwan, it was difficult to predict what would happen after five years.
China sporadically repeats its threat to retake Taiwan by force if the island declares independence, and consistently opposes sales of weapons to the island.

Beijing held war games and missile tests near Taiwan before the island's first direct presidential election in March 1996 in what Beijing acknowledged was a warning to Taiwanese voters not to drop a pledge to reunify eventually with the mainland.

Beijing has said that after Britain hands over Hong Kong in July and Portugal returns neighbouring Macau to Chinese sovereignty in December 1999, Taiwan will stand out in 2000 as the only blemish on its vision of a fully unified China.
